title: Margarita Hangover: Why It Hits So Hard and How to Avoid It
excerpt: Why margaritas cause such rough hangovers, how many drinks are really in one, frozen vs. rocks vs. skinny, a Cinco de Mayo game plan, and how to recover.
metaDescription: Why margaritas cause brutal hangovers, how many drinks are in one, which styles are worst, a Cinco de Mayo plan, and how to recover the next morning.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** margaritas give people rough hangovers mostly because of how much alcohol they hold and how easy they are to drink, not because tequila is uniquely evil. A classic margarita made with a full pour of tequila and an orange liqueur carries about two standard drinks. A big frozen or restaurant "grande" can hold more than that, and the lime, sugar, and salt hide the taste of the alcohol so well that it's easy to have three of them in the time you'd nurse one beer. Add cheap mixto tequila, sugary bottled mix, an afternoon in the sun, and salty, spicy food, and you have a near-perfect recipe for a pounding headache, an upset stomach, and a dry mouth the next day.

**The quick rules:** Count each margarita as at least two drinks. Ask for (or make) it with 100% agave tequila and fresh lime instead of neon-green mix. Eat a real meal before and during, alternate every margarita with a full glass of water, and stop well before you feel "done." If you're already hungover, rehydrate slowly, eat something bland, and give it time.

> **When to see a doctor:** Most margarita hangovers are miserable but harmless and fade within a day. **Get medical help right away (call 911 in the US)** if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, has slow or irregular breathing, has cold or bluish skin, has a seizure, or keeps vomiting while drowsy. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover, and they need care, not sleep. Also see a doctor if you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, see blood in vomit or stool, have severe belly pain that spreads to your back, or have chest pain or a racing heart that doesn't settle. And if you notice shaking, sweating, or anxiety that shows up every time you stop drinking after a stretch of heavy days, mention it to a doctor, because that pattern is worth checking even if it feels like an ordinary hangover.

## Why Margaritas Hit So Hard: It's Mostly the Math

Ask a group of people which drink gives them the worst hangover and "margaritas" or "tequila" will come up a lot. The reputation is real, but the main reason is less mysterious than it seems. It's how much alcohol is in the glass.

In the US, one standard drink is about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly a 12-ounce regular beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof (40%) spirit.

Now look at a classic margarita:

- **Tequila:** usually 1.5 to 2 ounces, at 40% alcohol
- **Orange liqueur (Cointreau or triple sec):** often 0.75 to 1 ounce. Cointreau is 40% alcohol, about the same as the tequila. Cheaper triple secs vary and are often weaker.
- **Lime juice and sweetener:** no alcohol, but plenty of flavor to cover the burn

Add the two spirits together and a well-made classic margarita often lands somewhere around 1.5 to 2 standard drinks. Nobody thinks of it that way. People count "one margarita" the same way they'd count one beer.

Then there are the restaurant versions. Large frozen margaritas, "grande" sizes, fishbowls, pitchers, and drinks with a beer or a "floater" shot upended into them can contain considerably more alcohol than a classic one. Pours vary a lot from bar to bar, so you often have no real idea how much tequila is in front of you. Three big margaritas over dinner can easily add up to six or more standard drinks, which is enough to give most people a hangover no matter what was in the glass.

### Why they go down so fast

A straight shot of tequila tastes like what it is. A margarita doesn't. The sour lime and sweetness mask the alcohol, the ice makes it cold and refreshing, and the salt rim makes you want another sip. Frozen margaritas are the most extreme version: they taste like a slushie, so people drink them at slushie speed.

Speed matters because your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for many adults (it varies with body size, sex, genetics, and other factors). Drink faster than that and your blood alcohol climbs. Higher peaks mean more dehydration, more disrupted sleep, and a worse morning.

## What's Actually Causing the Hangover

Hangovers come from several things happening at once. A margarita night tends to stack most of them.

### 1. The alcohol itself

This is the big one. When your liver breaks down alcohol, the first by-product is **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound that's linked to nausea, flushing, a racing heart, and that poisoned feeling. Alcohol also triggers inflammation, irritates the stomach lining, and wrecks the quality of your sleep, even if it helps you fall asleep. Researchers still argue about the exact mix of causes, but the total amount of alcohol is the most consistent predictor of how bad a hangover gets.

### 2. Dehydration and lost electrolytes

Alcohol blocks a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. So you pee more than you drink. Dehydration doesn't explain the whole hangover, but it contributes to the headache, thirst, dizziness, and dry mouth. For a deeper look, see our guide on [whether alcohol really dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

### 3. Congeners and the quality of the tequila

Congeners are by-products of fermentation and aging, such as methanol, other alcohols, and various flavor compounds. Darker, more heavily aged spirits like bourbon and brandy tend to have more of them than clear spirits like vodka. In a well-known study, people who drank bourbon reported somewhat worse hangovers than people who drank the same amount of vodka, though the difference was modest compared with the effect of the alcohol itself.

Tequila sits somewhere in the middle. Blanco (silver) tequila is unaged and fairly clean. Reposado and añejo are aged in barrels and pick up more congeners. The bigger issue for many margaritas is the type of tequila:

- **100% agave tequila** is made only from blue agave sugars. The bottle will say "100% de agave" or "100% agave."
- **Mixto tequila** only has to be at least 51% agave. The rest of the fermentable sugar can come from other sources, like cane sugar. Many cheap "gold" tequilas used in well drinks and frozen machines are mixtos, sometimes with added coloring and flavoring.

There's no good evidence that 100% agave tequila prevents hangovers, and the research comparing specific tequilas is thin. But a lot of people report feeling better after the 100% agave stuff, and it's a reasonable choice if you're drinking anyway. We cover this in more detail in [the truth about tequila hangovers](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth) and our [guide to congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

### 4. Sugar, mixes, and the orange liqueur

Bottled margarita mix and frozen-machine bases are often loaded with sugar, corn syrup, and artificial color. Sugar doesn't directly cause hangovers, and some of what you read online about "sugar hangovers" goes beyond the evidence. The real problems with sugary mixes are indirect:

- They hide the alcohol even more, so you drink faster.
- A big sugar load on an empty stomach can leave you feeling shaky and crashy later, on top of alcohol's own effect on blood sugar.
- Lots of sweet, acidic liquid can upset a stomach that alcohol is already irritating.

Fresh lime, a little agave syrup, and a measured pour of good orange liqueur makes a better drink and a smaller one. If you want to go further down this rabbit hole, our article on [the best mixers to avoid a hangover](/never-hungover/best-mixers-to-avoid-hangover) compares common options.

### 5. Salt, lime, spice, and your stomach

The salt rim adds a little sodium, which is not a bad thing on its own, but it also makes you thirstier and keeps you sipping. Lime juice is very acidic. Pair three or four margaritas with spicy salsa, chips, and a heavy plate of fried food, and plenty of people wake up with heartburn, a sour stomach, or diarrhea. If that's your main symptom, see our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking).

### 6. Sun, heat, and dancing

Margaritas are a patio, beach, pool, and festival drink. Drinking in the sun means you're losing extra water through sweat, and heat makes you thirsty for the cold drink in your hand rather than water. That combination is one reason daytime margarita sessions feel so much worse than the number of drinks suggests.

## Frozen vs. On the Rocks vs. Skinny: Which Is Worst?

There's no study ranking margarita styles by hangover, so this is based on how each one is usually made and served.

**Frozen margaritas.** Often the worst offenders in practice. They're easy to drink quickly, frequently made from sugary premix and cheaper tequila, and served in large glasses. The ice dilutes the flavor so you notice the alcohol less. The one point in their favor: some of the volume is just melted ice, which is water.

**On the rocks.** A margarita over ice, made with fresh lime, is usually a better bet. You can taste the drink, so you're more likely to sip it. But a strong pour on the rocks can still be two drinks or more.

**Straight up (shaken and served without ice).** Same alcohol, smaller glass, finished faster. Not inherently worse, but it goes quickly.

**Skinny margaritas.** Usually tequila, lime, and a little agave or soda water, without the orange liqueur. Less sugar and often a bit less alcohol, because the second spirit is gone. That can genuinely help, as long as the bar isn't making up for it with a heavier tequila pour.

**Spicy margaritas.** The jalapeño won't make your hangover worse by itself, but if your stomach is sensitive, spice plus lime plus alcohol is a rough mix.

**"Beer-rita" or margaritas with a bottle of beer flipped in.** These stack two drinks into one glass. Count them accordingly.

**Ranch water and margaritas with soda.** Some small studies suggest carbonated mixers may speed up how quickly alcohol is absorbed, though results are mixed. Ranch water (tequila, lime, and sparkling mineral water) is still a lighter drink than most margaritas, because it skips the liqueur and the sugar.

**Pitchers.** The hardest format to keep track of. People top up glasses before they're empty, and nobody knows how many they've had. If you share a pitcher, try to keep count yourself.

## The Cinco de Mayo Hangover

Cinco de Mayo is the most margarita-heavy day of the year in the US, and the hangover the next morning has become a running joke. It tends to be a bad one for reasons that go beyond the drinks themselves:

- **It often starts early.** Happy hours, lunch specials, and outdoor events mean many people start drinking in the afternoon, which stretches the session out over many hours.
- **It's usually outside.** Patios, parks, and street parties add sun and heat.
- **Bars get slammed.** Busy bartenders pour fast, frozen machines run nonstop, and pitchers and drink specials make it harder to track what you've had.
- **Shots join the party.** Tequila shots between margaritas can quietly double your total.
- **It often falls on a weeknight.** So many people go to work the next day on short, poor-quality sleep.

### A simple Cinco de Mayo game plan

1. **Eat a real meal before you start.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream. Tacos with protein and some fat are better than chips alone.
2. **Decide your number before you go.** Two margaritas is often four standard drinks. Pick a limit that fits what you have to do tomorrow.
3. **Start with water, not a margarita.** If you show up thirsty from the sun, your first drink will vanish in minutes.
4. **Match every margarita with a full glass of water.** Ask the bartender for water with every round.
5. **Order on the rocks with 100% agave tequila and fresh lime,** or a skinny version, rather than a frozen premix drink.
6. **Skip the shots.** Or, if you take one, count it as a drink and drop a margarita.
7. **Stay in the shade when you can.** Sweat plus alcohol is a fast route to feeling awful.
8. **Get home, drink water, and sleep as long as you can.** Your body needs time more than anything else.

## How to Recover From a Margarita Hangover

Nothing fixes a hangover quickly. Your body needs time to clear the alcohol and its by-products, and most hangovers improve within about a day (see [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last)). These steps can make the wait more bearable.

### Rehydrate slowly and steadily

Sip water rather than chugging it, especially if you feel queasy. If you sweated a lot or have been sick, a drink with electrolytes (sodium and potassium) can help, whether that's an oral rehydration drink, a sports drink, or a [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink). Skip another margarita "to take the edge off." Drinking more alcohol just delays the hangover.

### Eat something gentle

If your stomach is unsettled, start bland: toast, crackers, bananas, rice, eggs, or broth. Once you can manage that, a normal meal with some protein usually helps you feel steadier. If you'd overdone the salsa and lime the night before, go easy on acid and spice for a day. Our guide to [hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more ideas for a sour stomach.

### Be careful with painkillers

For a headache, ibuprofen or naproxen can help some people, but they can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already inflamed, so take them with food and stay within the label dose. Avoid acetaminophen (Tylenol) while there's still alcohol in your system or after a very heavy night, because both put load on the liver. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why. If you have stomach, kidney, or liver problems, or take other medicines, ask a pharmacist which option is right for you.

### Rest

Alcohol breaks up your sleep in the second half of the night, so you probably slept worse than you think. A nap, a slow morning, and an early night do more than most hangover hacks.

### Don't drive until you're truly sober

After a long margarita session, you can still have alcohol in your blood the next morning. If you drank heavily late into the night, give it plenty of time before you drive.

## How to Enjoy Margaritas Without Paying for It Tomorrow

You don't have to give up margaritas to have fewer bad mornings. Most of the difference comes from a few habits:

- **Make them yourself when you can.** A measured 1.5 ounces of 100% agave blanco, 0.75 ounce of orange liqueur, and fresh lime gives you a much clearer picture of what you're drinking than a restaurant grande.
- **Ask for a "short pour" or a skinny version** when you're out. Many bars will happily make one.
- **Go easy on the salt** if you find it keeps you sipping. Half-salt rims are an easy compromise.
- **Order a glass of water with every drink,** and actually finish it.
- **Slow down.** Aim for no more than about one standard drink an hour, which means one margarita every hour and a half to two hours, not one every 20 minutes.
- **Watch the tequila shots.** They're the fastest way to turn a good night into a bad morning.
- **Know your limit and keep track.** Pitchers and refills make this hard, so keep count on your phone if you need to.

If you're curious which tequilas people find easiest on them, our roundup of [the best tequila for no hangover](/never-hungover/best-tequila-for-no-hangover) goes brand by brand. And if margaritas are just one item on a long list of sugary drinks you're worried about, our list of [the worst cocktails for hangovers](/never-hungover/worst-cocktails-for-hangovers) covers the rest.

## Myths About Margarita and Tequila Hangovers

**"Tequila is an upper, so it doesn't give you a hangover."** Tequila is ethanol, just like every other alcoholic drink. It's a depressant, and it causes hangovers in proportion to how much you drink. Some people feel more energetic on tequila, but that's more about the setting and the expectations than the drink.

**"Good tequila means no hangover."** Better tequila may help a little by cutting down on congeners and additives, but there is no good evidence that any tequila stops a hangover when you drink a lot of it.

**"The salt rim keeps you hydrated."** The amount of salt on a rim is small, and alcohol's effect on your kidneys is much larger. Water is what keeps you hydrated.

**"Frozen margaritas are weaker."** Sometimes, but often not by as much as you'd think, and they tend to be bigger and faster to drink.

**"A margarita the next morning cures it."** "Hair of the dog" just delays the hangover by topping your blood alcohol back up. It doesn't speed up recovery.

**"Lime juice detoxes the alcohol."** Lime adds flavor and a bit of vitamin C. It doesn't change how your liver processes alcohol.

## Signs It's More Than a Hangover

It's worth knowing the difference between a bad hangover and something that needs medical help.

**Call 911 (in the US) or get emergency care** if someone who has been drinking:

- Is confused, can't be woken, or keeps passing out
- Has slow breathing (fewer than about eight breaths a minute) or long gaps between breaths
- Has pale, cold, or bluish skin
- Has a seizure
- Is vomiting while very drowsy or unconscious

Don't leave a person in that state to "sleep it off." Turn them on their side to protect their airway and stay with them until help arrives. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) walks through what to look for and what to do.

**See a doctor soon** if you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, have severe stomach pain (especially pain that spreads to your back), notice blood in vomit or stool, have a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't calm down, or feel faint when you stand up. And if you've been drinking heavily for several days in a row and notice shaking, sweating, or a racing heart when you stop, talk to a doctor. That can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal rather than an ordinary hangover, and it's safer to have it checked.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take before or while drinking. In animal studies, it has shown effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts in the brain, and some small studies suggest possible support for the liver. Human research is still limited, so it's best seen as an optional extra rather than a fix. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers on its own, and it won't make six margaritas feel like two.

If you want to try it alongside the habits above, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with other ingredients, and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a simpler, lower-cost option. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [guide to preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) explains what tends to make the biggest difference. If you take any medication or have a health condition, check with a doctor or pharmacist before adding a supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Margaritas give harsh hangovers mainly because each one often holds about two drinks' worth of alcohol, the lime and sugar make them go down fast, and they tend to be drunk in the sun alongside salty, spicy food. Cheap mixto tequila and sugary premix probably make things a bit worse, but the amount you drink matters far more than anything else. Choose 100% agave tequila and fresh lime, count each margarita as two drinks, eat first, match each one with water, and you'll still enjoy the night with a much better shot at a decent morning.

For how this drink compares with the rest, see our [ranking of alcohol from least to most hangover](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) and our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do margaritas give me such a bad hangover?**

Mostly because of how much alcohol they hold and how fast they go down. A classic margarita with tequila and orange liqueur is often around 1.5 to 2 standard drinks, and large restaurant or frozen versions can be more. The lime, sugar, and salt hide the alcohol, so it's easy to drink several quickly. Cheap mixto tequila, sugary premix, sun, and salty or spicy food can add to it.

**How many drinks are in a margarita?**

A classic margarita made with about 2 ounces of tequila and 1 ounce of a 40% orange liqueur like Cointreau contains roughly two US standard drinks. Smaller pours or weaker triple sec bring that down a little. Large, frozen, or 'grande' restaurant margaritas, and drinks with a beer or extra shot added, can contain more. Pours vary a lot by bar.

**Are frozen margaritas worse for hangovers?**

Often, in practice. They're usually made from sugary premix and cheaper tequila, served in big glasses, and taste like a slushie, so people drink them quickly. There's no study ranking margarita styles, but the speed and size are what make frozen ones risky. A margarita on the rocks with fresh lime is usually easier to pace.

**Does 100% agave tequila prevent a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that any tequila prevents a hangover. 100% agave tequila skips the non-agave sugars allowed in mixto tequila and many people report feeling better on it, so it's a reasonable choice if you're drinking. But the total amount of alcohol matters far more than the brand or type.

**How do I avoid a Cinco de Mayo hangover?**

Eat a real meal before you start, decide your limit ahead of time, and remember that two margaritas can be about four drinks. Order on the rocks with 100% agave tequila and fresh lime, skip the tequila shots, drink a full glass of water with every round, and stay out of the sun when you can. Get home with time to sleep, especially if you work the next day.

**Is a skinny margarita better for a hangover?**

It can be a little better. Skinny margaritas usually drop the orange liqueur and most of the sugar, which means less alcohol and less sweetness masking it. That only helps if the bar doesn't add extra tequila to make up for it, and you still need to pace yourself.

**What's the best thing to do for a margarita hangover?**

Sip water steadily, add an electrolyte drink if you sweated a lot or were sick, eat something bland like toast, eggs, or broth, and rest. Go easy on acid and spice for a day if your stomach is sour. If you use a pain reliever, take ibuprofen with food and avoid acetaminophen while alcohol may still be in your system. Time is the only thing that fully clears a hangover.

**When is a margarita hangover a reason to see a doctor?**

Get emergency help if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, has slow or irregular breathing, has cold or bluish skin, has a seizure, or vomits while drowsy. See a doctor if you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, have severe belly pain, see blood in vomit or stool, or have a racing heart that won't settle.
